content: Medications selected for the treatment of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) should demonstrate an efficacy of at least 95%. The criteria for selecting these medications are outlined in Box 1. Recommended medications should meet as many of these criteria as possible, considering factors such as local availability, efficacy, the route and frequency of administration, and cost. Identifying and Procuring STI Medications It is essential to identify first-line treatment options for STIs and estimate the quantities of medications required. Quantifying medication needs is critical for cost estimation, aligning financial requirements with available budgets, and placing orders in advance to minimize unit and freight costs. To estimate the required quantities, it is necessary to review the recommended medications, their unit prices, the amount needed per treatment, and epidemiological data on infection prevalence. Medication needs can be calculated by multiplying the estimated number of cases by the total quantity of medication required for one case. Data from health centers providing care should be verified to avoid over-ordering and wastage. Budgeting for medications is crucial. If the national health ministry does not provide free medications and patients cannot afford them, controlling the spread of infection and preventing complications becomes nearly impossible. At the national level, decision-makers, politicians, and financial controllers must understand the importance of subsidizing STI medications. Low-cost STI medications can be sourced through international generic vendors, non-profit procurement schemes (e.g., UNICEF, UNFPA, UNHCR), and joint procurement programs. These schemes allow national programs to collaborate with others, reducing overall costs by sharing overhead expenses and benefiting from bulk purchase discounts. Including STI medications on national essential medicines lists increases the likelihood of obtaining these medications at low costs. STI Treatment for Key Populations Key populations, such as sex workers, men who have sex with men (MSM), and individuals living with HIV, are at higher risk of acquiring and transmitting STIs, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Increasing access to STI services, including treatment for specific infections, is critical for these groups. WHO guidelines provide recommendations for improving access and delivering STI services to key populations. These include practical approaches for comprehensive HIV/STI programs targeting sex workers, MSM, and other vulnerable groups. Criteria for Selecting STI Medications Medications for STI treatment should meet the following criteria: High efficacy (≥95% cure rate) High quality (potent active ingredients) Low cost Low toxicity Minimal likelihood of resistance development Single-dose administration Oral administration Safe for use in pregnant or lactating women Appropriate medications should be included in national essential medicines lists, and the competencies of healthcare providers should be considered when selecting treatments. Treatment of Gonococcal Infections The WHO recommends that local antimicrobial resistance (AMR) data guide the choice of therapy for gonococcal infections. In settings without local resistance data, dual therapy is preferred over single therapy. Dual therapy options include: Ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly (IM) as a single dose plus azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose Cefixime 400 mg orally as a single dose plus azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose Single therapy options, based on local resistance data, include: Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM as a single dose Cefixime 400 mg orally as a single dose Spectinomycin 2 g IM as a single dose (not for oropharyngeal infections) Due to emerging resistance, quinolones are no longer recommended for gonococcal infections. Dual therapy is favored because of resistance concerns and limited surveillance data. Additional studies comparing dual therapy combinations (e.g., gentamicin, ceftriaxone, cefixime, or gemifloxacin with azithromycin) are needed to inform future recommendations. Retreatment After Treatment Failure For individuals with gonococcal infections who fail initial treatment, the following options are suggested: If reinfection is suspected, retreat with a WHO-recommended regimen, reinforce condom use or abstinence, and provide partner treatment. If treatment failure occurs after a non-WHO-recommended regimen, retreat with a WHO-recommended regimen. If resistance data are available, retreat according to susceptibility. If failure occurs after WHO-recommended single therapy, retreat with dual therapy. If failure occurs after dual therapy, retreat with higher doses of dual therapy (e.g., ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 2 g orally). Before retreatment, reinfection should be distinguished from treatment failure, and resistance data should be obtained when possible. Ophthalmia Neonatorum For neonates with gonococcal conjunctivitis, the WHO suggests one of the following treatments: Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (maximum 150 mg) IM as a single dose Kanamycin 25 mg/kg (maximum 75 mg) IM as a single dose Spectinomycin 25 mg/kg (maximum 75 mg) IM as a single dose Topical ocular prophylaxis is recommended for all neonates to prevent gonococcal and chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum. Options include: Povidone iodine 2.5% solution (water-based) Silver nitrate 1% solution Chloramphenicol 1% eye ointment Prophylaxis should be administered immediately after birth. Alcohol-based povidone iodine must not be used due to the risk of harm. Research Implications Research is urgently needed to address increasing AMR in gonococcal infections. Randomized controlled trials should evaluate new treatment options, dual therapy combinations, and alternatives such as gentamicin and kanamycin. Studies should include diverse populations, including MSM and sex workers, and focus on treatment failure, distinguishing between reinfection and resistance. Surveillance of AMR and the effectiveness of ocular prophylaxis in neonates should also be prioritized.
